nugatory

NOO-guh-tor-ee · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Nugatory is of no real value, importance, or impact.

Without any real enforcement power, the committee's ruling was largely nugatory.

Example

Critics called the reform nugatory, since the loopholes it left in place made the new rule meaningless in practice.

The rule technically existed, but it accomplished nothing real -- which is exactly what nugatory describes.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

worthless: Worthless means having no value at all — nothing about the thing is good, useful, or worth keeping. Nugatory is a different verdict: a nugatory rule or plan can be admired, even praised, and still produce no practical effect whatsoever. Worth is about quality; impact is the nugatory question.

ineffectual: Ineffectual describes an effort or person that tries and fails to produce the intended result — an ineffectual protest, an ineffectual apology. Nugatory is the colder, more formal verdict on a thing's status: it does not try and fail; it simply carries no practical impact at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

consequential: having significant importance or impact

Where it sits · how little effect it actually has

minor → nugatory → void

minor vs. nugatory: Something minor still has some impact, just a small one; something nugatory has essentially no impact at all.

void vs. nugatory: Nugatory describes something that accomplishes nothing in practice; void means it has no legal force at all.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — nugator: a trifler, joker (Latin (nugator))

suffix — -y: relating to, characterized by (Latin)

Put it together: Nugatory comes from Latin nugae ('jokes, trifles') + -tory -- describing something as trifling or worthless.

Use the root in a new word: nugatory: Latin nugae left little trace in everyday English beyond words built directly on nugatory itself -- one of the rarer roots that stayed almost entirely inside its own word family.
